The readings that differ most on this verse: Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Reformed, and the historical-critical reading.

## Catholic
Peter himself is the rock. Jesus gives Simon a new name and then builds on him, so the Church rests on Peter's person and office, which passes to the bishops of Rome who succeed him. The weight falls on the wordplay between Peter and rock, read as one and the same, and on the promise that Hades will not prevail. It assumes Scripture fully true, the promise a real act of Christ, and tradition and council as the authority that reads the text, which makes it conservative in the theological sense. Held by the Catholic Church.

## Eastern Orthodox
The rock is Peter's confession in the verse before, and Peter as the one who confesses it. Many of the Fathers read it so, and Orthodox teaching holds that every bishop who keeps that confession sits in Peter's seat, so the verse founds the Church on right faith and on the whole episcopate. The weight falls on the confession and on the shift from Petros to petra. It assumes Scripture fully true, the promise a real act of Christ, and the Fathers as authority, which makes it conservative on the same counts. Held by the Orthodox Churches.

## Reformed
The rock is Christ, confessed by Peter, who speaks for all the apostles; the Church is built on that confession, so no single office is founded here. The weight falls on the change of word from Petros to petra and on Scripture read with Scripture, where Christ is the one foundation (1 Corinthians 3:11) and the living stone (1 Peter 2:4–8). It assumes Scripture fully true, the promise a real act of Christ, and the text alone as authority, which makes it conservative on Scripture and the supernatural. Held by Reformed and Presbyterian churches, and by most evangelical churches.

## Historical-critical
The saying is read as Matthew's community reflecting on Peter's standing after his death: Matthew alone uses the word assembly, and alone records this promise. Some scholars defend it as an original saying, perhaps in Aramaic, where one word, Kepha, would stand for both name and rock. It assumes Scripture a human record, the promise a story told for the community, and scholarly reconstruction as authority, which makes it liberal in the theological sense on both counts.

## Where they agree
All four read Peter as spokesman for the apostles' confession, the assembly as the one people Jesus gathers, and the gates of Hades as the power of death, which cannot destroy it.

## Where they part, and why
- Whether Petros and petra name the same thing: one rock for the Catholic reading, a shift that matters for the others.
- Whether what is founded is an office that passes on, a confession kept by all bishops, or the confession as such.
- Whether the words are Jesus' own or the community's: an assumption about Scripture.
- What settles it: tradition, the Fathers, Scripture read with Scripture, or reconstruction.

## What the text settles
The wordplay is in the text, and the confession stands in the verse before it, so a reading that separates the rock from the confession rests on little here. The Greek has two forms, Petros and petra, and the passage does not say whether the change is meant. Nothing in the verse speaks of succession, for or against.

## Questions to take back to the text
1. Read verses 13 to 20 together: does the promise answer the man or the confession?
2. In your translation, is rock the same word as Peter, and what changes if it is?
3. What does Jesus build, an assembly, and who belongs to it elsewhere in this Gospel?
